QUESTION:
How much did the Year 8 small-group maths tutoring programme improve tutored students' test scores, and would making it compulsory for the whole year group raise average attainment?

DATA:
Year 8 maths tutoring programme, one school, 2024-25.

In September, teachers nominated 75 students they considered to be struggling in maths. These students were offered small-group tutoring (two sessions a week, September to May). The other 140 Year 8 students were not tutored. All students sit the same standardised maths test (scored 0-100) in autumn and in summer.

| Group | Students with both tests | Autumn mean | Summer mean |
| Tutored | 60 | 42 | 54 |
| Not tutored | 140 | 58 | 63 |

15 of the 75 nominated students left the programme before summer (moved school, stopped attending, or were withdrawn by parents). They are excluded from the table above. Their autumn mean was 35. 11 of the 15 were still at the school and sat the summer test; their summer mean was 38.

Test publisher's note: the autumn-to-summer test-retest correlation is about 0.7. Students selected because of low scores on one sitting typically score closer to the average on the next sitting, even without any intervention.

The school is considering making tutoring compulsory for all 215 Year 8 students next year.

KNOWN FLAWS:
F1. [misreport] The data says students were nominated by teachers because they were struggling, not randomly allocated. Selection on low scores also brings regression to the mean (the publisher's note). CORRECTION: This is a non-randomised comparison of a low-scoring selected group with everyone else. Group differences cannot be attributed cleanly to the programme, and part of the tutored gain is expected regression to the mean.
F2. [method] Uses the raw pre-post gain and ignores the comparison group's gain of 5 points, i.e. ignores the baseline improvement everyone made. CORRECTION: Difference-in-differences: 12 − 5 = 7 points (the draft itself notes the gap narrowed by 7). Even this is an upper bound, given regression to the mean.
F3. [omission] Ignores the 15 nominated students who left the programme. They started lower (autumn mean 35), and the 11 who were tested gained only 3 points. Excluding them inflates the tutored group's gain. CORRECTION: Including the 11 tested leavers (intention to treat): autumn mean 2,905/71 = 40.9, summer 3,658/71 = 51.5, gain 10.6. DiD 10.6 − 5 = about 5.6 points, before any allowance for regression to the mean.
F4. [inference] Generalises an effect estimated on teacher-nominated low-attaining students to the whole year group, including higher attainers, and to a compulsory programme. CORRECTION: The data cannot support any estimate for students who were not struggling or for a compulsory programme. At most, a modest effect on nominated low attainers is suggested.

EXTENSIONS:
- Estimate the regression-to-the-mean component. With a test-retest correlation of 0.7 and a cohort mean of about 53 in autumn ((60×42 + 140×58)/200 = 53.2), a group 11 points below the mean would be expected to move about 0.3 × 11, or roughly 3 points, towards it without any intervention. This shrinks the DiD estimate further.
- Propose a stronger design for next year: randomise tutoring among nominated students (or use a waiting list), which would let the school estimate the effect without selection bias.
- Report the distribution, not just means: e.g. the proportion of tutored students moving above a pass threshold, and whether gains were concentrated among a few students.

FINAL VERSION:
# Year 8 Maths Tutoring: Impact Evaluation

## Summary

- **The 12-point rise for tutored students overstates what the programme achieved.** Three other things contribute to it:
  - **Ordinary progress.** Untutored students gained 5 points without any tutoring.
  - **Regression to the mean.** Students chosen because they scored low tend to score closer to the average next time, even with no help.
  - **Selective dropout.** The 15 students who left were doing worse than the others, and the headline figure leaves them out.
- **For the 60 students who completed tutoring, the best estimate of the effect is about 2 to 7 points.** The two figures come from two standard methods. They disagree because the groups started 16 points apart. Which one is right depends on how teachers chose students, and the data cannot settle that.
- **Across everyone offered tutoring, the estimate is about 0 to 6 points.** If the 4 leavers with no summer score are counted, it may be nearer 0 to 5. At the low end, the programme had essentially no average effect.
- **The data cannot show that compulsory tutoring for all 215 students would raise the year-group average.** Even taken at face value, targeted tutoring moves the year average by only about 0 to 2 points, and the current programme already delivers that. There is no evidence at all on how the other 140 students would respond.
- **Recommendation:** do not make tutoring compulsory on this evidence. Keep targeted tutoring and evaluate it properly, ideally by allocating borderline places by lottery or by pooling cohorts.

## What kind of study this is

Students were **not** randomly allocated:

- In September, teachers nominated 75 students they judged to be struggling.
- All 75 were offered small-group tutoring, twice a week from September to May.
- The other 140 students were not tutored.

The two groups were different from the start. Their autumn scores were 16 points apart, and they probably also differed in motivation and home support. So differences in progress cannot simply be credited to tutoring.

All students sat the same standardised test (scored 0–100) in autumn and in summer.

## Results

| Group | Students with both tests | Autumn | Summer | Change |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tutored (completed) | 60 | 42 | 54 | +12 |
| Not tutored | 140 | 58 | 63 | +5 |
| Left programme | 15 (11 sat summer) | 35 | 38 | about +3* |
| All nominated who sat summer | 71 | 40.9* | 51.5 | about +10.6* |

\*Assumes the 11 leavers who sat the summer test had the same autumn mean (35) as all 15 leavers. This could not be checked.

Reference points:

- Whole year group, autumn mean: 51.9 (215 students).
- Summer mean for the 211 students who sat it: 59.1.
- All 75 nominated students, autumn mean: 40.6.

## Estimating the effect

There are two standard ways to compare groups that started at different levels. Here they give different answers.

### 1. Comparing gains (difference-in-differences): about 7 points

This method subtracts the untutored group's progress from the tutored group's progress: **12 − 5 = 7 points.**

It assumes **parallel trends**: without tutoring, struggling students would have gained the same 5 points as everyone else. That assumption can fail in either direction:

- **If lower attainers normally make slower progress,** the true effect is larger than 7.
- **If lower scorers had more room to improve,** for example because stronger students were nearer the top of the scale, then 5 points understates their normal progress and the true effect is smaller than 7.

### 2. Adjusting for the starting score (ANCOVA): about 2 points

This method predicts each group's summer score from its autumn score, which builds in regression to the mean. The test publisher reports an autumn-to-summer correlation of about 0.7. Assuming the scores are similarly spread on both sittings, a gap between two groups in autumn should shrink to about 0.7 times that gap by summer if tutoring had no effect.

- In autumn, completers scored 42 and untutored students 58, a gap of −16 points.
- With no tutoring effect, the expected summer gap is 0.7 × (−16) = −11.2 points.
- The observed summer gap was 54 − 63 = −9 points.
- **Effect ≈ −9 − (−11.2) = 2.2 points.**

The same calculation can be expressed as a predicted score:

- From the untutored group, a student starting at the year-group autumn mean would be expected to score about 58.7 in summer.
- Completers started 9.9 points below that mean, so with no tutoring effect they would be expected to score about 58.7 − 0.7 × 9.9 ≈ 51.8.
- They actually scored 54.

### Why the two methods disagree, and which applies

This is a well-known problem, often called **Lord's paradox**. When groups start far apart, comparing gains and adjusting for starting scores can give quite different answers. The right method depends on how students were chosen:

- **If nomination was driven mainly by the autumn test,** or by recent work that has the same random ups and downs, then part of the tutored group's low autumn score was bad luck that would have reversed anyway. Adjusting for the starting score is the right approach, and the effect is about 2 points.
- **If teachers relied on stable, longer-term evidence,** the tutored group's low scores reflect genuinely lower attainment that would not reverse by itself. Then the adjustment over-corrects, comparing gains is the better approach, and the effect is nearer 7 points.

Teacher nomination was probably a mix of the two, so the true effect probably lies somewhere between 2 and 7. **The 2-to-7 range is a choice between two plausible models, not a firm bound.** The assumptions behind either model could be wrong.

### 3. Students who left

The 15 leavers matter more than their numbers suggest.

- They started 16.9 points below the year mean. With no tutoring effect, the adjusted model predicts a summer score of about 58.7 − 0.7 × 16.9 ≈ **47**.
- The 11 who sat the summer test scored **38**, about 9 points below that prediction.
- They also fell short of the gain-based prediction of 35 + 5 = 40.

So **dropout was selective**. The students who left were doing worse than expected. Leaving them out makes the remaining 60 look better than the programme deserves.

**The leavers' score of 38 should not be read as evidence that tutoring harmed them.** Students left for different reasons, such as stopping attending or being withdrawn by parents. Each of these may reflect wider disengagement from school or difficulties at home rather than a reaction to tutoring. The point is only that the students who completed are a favourable subset.

### 4. Counting everyone who was offered tutoring

A fairer estimate includes everyone offered tutoring, not just those who completed it. This is called an **intention-to-treat** estimate. Using the 71 nominated students who sat the summer test:

- **Adjusted for starting score:** the expected summer score with no effect is 58.7 − 0.7 × 11.0 ≈ 51.0, and the observed score was 51.5. **Effect ≈ 0.5 points.**
- **Comparing gains:** 10.6 − 5 = **5.6 points.**

**Estimate for everyone offered tutoring: about 0 to 6 points.**

This probably still overstates the effect, because 4 leavers have no summer score. Most likely they are the students who moved school. The table below assumes they performed like the other 11 leavers:

| Method | Effect if the 4 missing leavers are included |
|---|---|
| Adjusted for starting score | about 0.0 points |
| Comparing gains | about 5.2 points |

If moving school was unrelated to how these students were doing, the overstatement is smaller. Either way, there are only four of them, so the range barely moves: **roughly 0 to 5–6 points.**

### 5. How precise these estimates are

Standard deviations were not reported, so a proper confidence interval cannot be calculated. The figures below are illustrative rather than measured. They assume a standard deviation of about 15 points, which is typical for a 0–100 test.

| Method | Relevant standard deviation | Standard error (60 vs 140) | 95% margin |
|---|---|---|---|
| Comparing gains | 15 × √(2 × 0.3) ≈ 11.6 | ≈ 1.8 | ≈ ±3.5 |
| Adjusted for starting score | 15 × √(1 − 0.49) ≈ 10.7 | ≈ 1.65 | ≈ ±3.2 |

These figures treat the 60 tutored students as independent, which makes the estimates look more precise than they are. Tutoring was delivered in **small groups**, so students in the same group shared a tutor, a timetable slot and group dynamics, and their results tend to move together.

- Suppose there were about 10 groups of 6 students and a modest within-group correlation of 0.1.
- The standard error would then rise by roughly 15 to 20%, giving a 95% margin of about ±4 points.
- With fewer groups or stronger differences between tutors, the margin would be wider.

On these assumptions:

- **A 2-point effect** is about one standard error from zero, so it cannot be told apart from chance.
- **A 7-point effect** would be clearly above zero.

The data therefore **cannot distinguish a modest real effect from no effect.**

### Bottom line on effect size

Tutoring may have given struggling students a modest benefit of a few points. It almost certainly did not add 12 points. That would require these students to have made no progress at all without tutoring, while their classmates gained 5 points. Once dropout is taken into account, an average effect close to zero cannot be ruled out.

## Would compulsory tutoring raise the year-group average?

This evaluation cannot show that it would, for five reasons.

1. **The gain is small even in the best case.** Nominated students are about 35% of the year (75 of 215). With an effect of 0 to 6 points for everyone offered tutoring, targeted tutoring moves the year-group average by about 0.35 × (0 to 6) ≈ **0 to 2 points**. The current targeted programme *already* delivers that. Making tutoring compulsory would add only whatever it does for the other 140 students.
2. **There is no evidence about the other 140 students.** Nothing in the data shows how students scoring 60 to 90 respond to tutoring. Extra small-group sessions could help them, make no difference, or crowd out more useful learning. A negative effect cannot be ruled out.
3. **Compulsion changes engagement.** Even in a voluntary programme, 20% of nominated students left. Those who stayed were probably the more willing ones. A compulsory programme would also include students who do not want to be there.
4. **Quality may fall at scale.** Covering 215 students instead of 75 roughly triples the number of groups. That needs more tutors and a reorganised timetable, and session quality may not hold up.
5. **Any forecast of a large year-group gain is unsupported** by these data.

## Costs and practicalities

Twice-weekly sessions from September to May are a substantial commitment. Extending them to every student would mean recruiting or redeploying tutors, restructuring the timetable, and giving up time now used for other things. The benefit is uncertain for struggling students and has no evidence behind it for everyone else, so the case for scaling up is weak.

## Recommendations

1. **Do not make tutoring compulsory for the whole year group** on this evidence.
2. **Keep targeted tutoring, but design next year's programme so it can show whether tutoring works.**
3. **Build in a fair comparison with enough students.** A single school's cohort is small, so the design needs to be able to produce a usable answer:
   - **Lottery among borderline students (preferred).** Guarantee places for the weakest students, and allocate places by lottery among a borderline band. This gives a clean comparison and a rationale that can be explained to parents.
   - **Score cut-off.** Offer tutoring to everyone below a fixed score and compare students just either side of it (a regression discontinuity design). In a year of about 215 students, only a few dozen would fall near the cut-off, so a single year's estimate would be very imprecise. It would also apply only to students near the threshold. Use this design only if cohorts or partner schools are pooled.
4. **Select students on more than one measure,** for example prior attainment as well as the autumn test. This reduces distortion from regression to the mean. If a cut-off is used, combine the measures into a single composite score, with the threshold fixed in advance.
5. **Track every nominated student, including those who leave.** Record why they left, which sessions they attended, and a summer score wherever possible. This allows a full analysis of everyone offered tutoring and a check on whether attending more sessions goes with larger gains.
6. **Record which tutoring group each student is in,** so the analysis can account for students in the same group performing alike.
7. **Report standard deviations and confidence intervals,** so the precision of any estimate is clear.
8. **To test tutoring for stronger students,** pilot it with a randomly chosen subset before committing the whole year group.
